growth_story.headline: Belize's income per person is about where it first was in 2003: a debt-fuelled boom, a long slide, then a pandemic collapse and a tourism-led rebound.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2004 income per person grew 3.6 percent a year, in growth spurts the IMF ties to tourism, investment and public spending, the later one paid for with rising foreign public debt. From 2005 to 2017 it shrank 0.8 percent a year: Belize's trade preferences in Europe eroded, natural disasters came more often and the government went through repeated debt restructurings, while the population grew faster than output. Income per person peaked in 2007, fell every year from 2008 to 2011, and fell again in 2016 and 2017. Since 2018 it has grown 1.6 percent a year, but that average hides the pandemic: income per person dropped 14.6 percent in 2020, then rose 16.6 percent in 2021 and 7.2 percent in 2022 as trade, tourism and business services came back. It fell 1.5 percent in 2023 and grew 2.0 percent in 2024 and 1.3 percent in 2025, leaving income per person 1.4 percent below its 2007 peak and about where it first was in 2003.

threads.title: Debt-financed booms, then restructurings
threads.text: The IMF describes two growth spurts before the mid-2000s, driven by tourism and investment, with the second financed by foreign public debt as private saving fell. That debt was restructured in 2006-2007, 2012-2013 and 2016-2017, which the IMF says hurt the government's credibility and its access to markets.

threads.title: Lost preferences and natural disasters
threads.text: From the mid-2000s, the IMF points to outside shocks: Belize's preferential access to European markets eroded, aid declined and natural disasters became more frequent. The IMF also finds that productivity fell from 2000 to 2016, as it did in other Caribbean economies.

citations.title: Reinvigorating Growth in Belize (IMF Working Paper WP/19/24)
citations.quote: The adverse external shocks include the erosion of preferential trade access to European markets, the decline of official development assistance, and increasingly frequent natural disasters.

citations.title: Reinvigorating Growth in Belize (IMF Working Paper WP/19/24)

threads.title: A population outgrowing output
threads.text: Belize's population has grown fast. After 2010 the economy as a whole kept growing, but the IMF estimated that the population grew faster, so income per person declined.

citations.title: Reinvigorating Growth in Belize (IMF Working Paper WP/19/24)
citations.quote: With average population growth estimated at about 2.5 percent per year, GDP per capita since 2010 has been declining

threads.title: Pandemic collapse and tourism rebound
threads.text: Services, especially tourism, drive much of Belize's economy, and output fell sharply in 2020. The rebound that followed was led by retail and wholesale trade, tourism and business process outsourcing, and the IMF reports that growth stayed strong through 2024.

citations.title: Belize: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2023 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: Key drivers of the rebound: retail and wholesale trade, tourism, and business process outsourcing.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2025 Article IV Consultation with Belize
citations.quote: Real GDP expanded by 30.6 percent between 2021 and 2023 and grew by 8.1 percent in 2024.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Belize (October 2026)

threads.title: Lower debt, exposure to fuel prices
threads.text: Public debt fell steeply from 2020 to 2025, helped by strong growth, tighter budgets and the 2021 debt-for-nature swap. Belize still imports energy and ties its currency to the U.S. dollar, which leaves it exposed to swings in world fuel prices.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Belize (October 2026)
citations.quote: Fiscal discipline, robust growth, and the 2021 debt-for-nature swap reduced public debt from about 103 percent of GDP in 2020 to 69.9 percent in 2025

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Belize (October 2026)
citations.quote: As a net energy importer operating under a U.S. dollar peg, the country is exposed to global fuel price fluctuations

since_last_year.text: Growth slowed in 2025, which the World Bank ties to weaker outside demand, and income per person rose 1.3 percent. In late 2025 the government bought the hydroelectric plants on the Macal River, which raised public debt for a time before the shares were sold to the public. In 2026 higher food and fuel prices pushed inflation back up.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes a strong rebound from 2021 through 2024, but in the data income per person in 2025 is still 1.4 percent below its 2007 peak and about where it first was in 2003. Much of the rebound only made up the 14.6 percent fall of 2020, and income per person fell 1.5 percent in 2023, inside the period the IMF counts as strong growth. The sources also disagree with each other: the World Bank's October 2026 figures put 2024 growth well below the IMF's 2025 figure, and the data show income per person grew 2.0 percent that year.
